headline: A Planet Too Hot to Reach, Ice That Holds Firm and a Black Hole's Hidden Diet
teaser: Why is the closest planet to the Sun so hard to reach? Will Antarctica's tallest ice cliffs really collapse? And what is quietly feeding the black hole at the heart of our galaxy?

articles.title: After an Eight-Year Journey, BepiColombo Reaches Mercury
articles.dek: A joint European-Japanese probe has arrived at the solar system's innermost planet, but is a slow, costly mission to Mercury the best use of space science money?

sources.name: ESA, latest updates on BepiColombo's arrival (Oct-Nov 2026)
BBC Sky at Night Magazine, 19 Oct 2026

paras: On 21 November 2026, a spacecraft that left Earth in October 2018 was scheduled to perform the most delicate maneuver of its long life: allowing the gravity of Mercury, the smallest planet in the solar system, to capture it into orbit. The mission, called BepiColombo, is a partnership between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). If all goes to plan, it will become only the second mission ever to orbit Mercury, and the first to place two separate orbiters around the planet at the same time.

Mercury may look like an easy target, since it is much closer to Earth than Jupiter or Saturn. In reality, it is one of the hardest places in the solar system to reach. Anything that falls toward the Sun speeds up, just as a ball gains speed rolling downhill. A spacecraft heading for Mercury therefore arrives far too fast, and the planet's weak gravity cannot hold on to it. As ESA flight dynamics expert Frank Budnik explained, BepiColombo "has to move at almost the same velocity as Mercury" before it can enter orbit. In other words, the real challenge is not going fast but slowing down.

To shed that excess speed without carrying an enormous load of fuel, engineers combined two techniques. The first was solar electric propulsion: a separate Mercury Transfer Module used electricity from large solar panels to power thrusters that gave gentle but continuous pushes for years. The second was a series of nine gravity-assist flybys, one past Earth, two past Venus and six past Mercury itself, each of which used a planet's gravity to bend the spacecraft's path and drain away some of its energy. The approach was elegant but slow, which is why the journey took eight years rather than a few months.

The journey did not always go smoothly. In April 2024, a problem with the solar panels reduced the power available to the electric thrusters. Engineers designed a new, lower-thrust route that saved the mission but pushed its arrival back from December 2025 to November 2026. Then, on 3 September 2026, the transfer module was released, leaving the two science orbiters still joined together, more than 200 million kilometers from Earth. Over the following weeks, the team switched on instruments for the first time; a laser altimeter, for example, fired more than 700,000 pulses in less than a day.

After capture, the work divides between the two partners. In early December, JAXA's Mio orbiter is due to separate and settle into a wide, elliptical orbit that takes about 9.3 hours to complete, from which it will study Mercury's magnetic field and how it interacts with the solar wind, the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter, carrying 11 science instruments, will gradually lower itself into a tight polar orbit of about 2.3 hours, reaching its final path in March 2027. Full science operations are planned to begin in April 2027 and to last at least a year.

Scientists hope the mission will help solve several puzzles. Mercury's iron core is enormous, filling more than half of the planet's volume, and nobody knows why. The planet also has a magnetic field, roughly 100 times weaker than Earth's, which is surprising for such a small world. NASA's MESSENGER probe, which orbited Mercury from 2011 to 2015, found ice hidden in permanently shadowed craters near the poles and strange shallow pits called hollows, and it added to evidence that the whole planet has shrunk by a few kilometers as its interior cooled. BepiColombo's sharper instruments should reveal far more.

Not everyone sees such missions as a priority. Critics point out that robotic exploration of distant planets is expensive and slow, and that a project which takes eight years merely to arrive may deliver results long after the questions that inspired it have changed. Some argue that the same money could do more good if spent on satellites that monitor Earth's climate, crops and oceans. International partnerships, they add, can multiply delays, because two agencies must coordinate budgets, designs and decisions.

Supporters reply that understanding Mercury is not a luxury. Astronomers have found thousands of planets orbiting other stars, and many of them circle extremely close to their suns, so Mercury is the nearest example of a world shaped by intense heat and radiation. Learning how it formed tests our theories of how planetary systems, including our own, came to be. Moreover, sharing a mission spreads the costs and risks, and building hardware that survives temperatures from about minus 170 to 430 degrees Celsius pushes engineering forward. In that sense, the long, patient trip to Mercury may be justified as much by what it teaches on the way as by what it finds.

speak.p: Some people think space agencies should spend their money on missions to distant planets such as Mercury. Others think the money should go to satellites that study Earth's climate and environment. Which do you think is more important, and why?
speak.hint: Choose one side; give two reasons (e.g., scientific knowledge vs urgent problems on Earth) and one example from the article; finish with a one-sentence conclusion.

write.p:
Dr. Lin: This week a European-Japanese spacecraft arrived at Mercury after an eight-year trip. Missions like this are slow and expensive, and they often depend on several countries working together. Do you think international partnerships are the best way to explore space, or should countries run their own missions? Why?
Emma: "Partnerships make sense. Space missions cost so much that sharing the bill lets countries do projects none of them could afford alone. Working together also builds trust between nations."
Kevin: "I'm less sure. When two agencies have to agree on every decision, projects get delayed. A country running its own mission can move faster and keep full control of the technology."
steps: State whether you favor partnerships or national missions.
Respond to Emma or Kevin and add a new reason of your own.
Support your view with an example, such as BepiColombo.
End with a short concluding sentence.

articles.title: Antarctica's Ice Cliffs May Be Less Likely to Collapse Than Feared
articles.dek: Satellite data suggest Antarctica's tallest ice cliffs stabilize after collapsing, but does good news about one risk mean we can relax about sea-level rise?
paras: Along the edges of Antarctica, glaciers end in towering walls of ice that rise straight out of the sea. For roughly a decade, some climate scientists have worried that these ice cliffs could become the weak point of the entire continent. A new study published in the journal Science in November 2026 suggests that the danger, while real, may be less dramatic than some computer models predicted. Using satellite measurements of more than 15,000 cliffs, researchers found that collapsing cliffs retreat quickly at first but then tend to stabilize, rather than crumbling in an unstoppable chain reaction.

The concern rests on an idea known as marine ice cliff instability, or MICI. According to this theory, a very tall wall of ice may be unable to support its own weight. If it breaks off, it can expose an even taller wall behind it, which may then collapse in turn, and the process can repeat itself again and again. Earlier studies, based mainly on computer models and a limited number of observations, suggested that cliffs taller than about 100 meters, roughly the height of a 30-story building, were especially vulnerable. Because Antarctica holds enough ice to raise global sea levels by dozens of meters, even a partial runaway collapse would threaten coastal cities around the world.

To test the theory against reality, Caroline Needell, a graduate student in a joint program of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, worked with Catherine Walker of Woods Hole and Jeremy Bassis of the University of Michigan. They used data from NASA's ICESat-2 satellite, which fires laser pulses at the ground to measure surface height with great precision. By analyzing measurements from 2019 to 2023, the team tracked thousands of cliffs every three months. The average cliff was about 30 meters tall, and only a small number exceeded the 100-meter threshold.

The researchers then examined four sites where cliffs reached about 100 meters, with the tallest measuring 127 meters. Here, the results contained surprises in both directions. When these cliffs collapsed, they retreated even faster than MICI models had predicted. Yet the retreat was short-lived: every glacier eventually stabilized, and some even advanced back toward the sea. "It's this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization," Needell said. "We don't see this runaway effect."

Several natural brakes appear to explain why. In front of many cliffs floats mélange, a slushy mixture of sea ice and broken icebergs, and the team found that taller cliffs tended to have thicker mélange, which may help hold them up. Deeper water in front of a cliff can also push back against the ice. The shape of the ground beneath the glacier matters too: where the bed rises, the ice becomes thinner, and cliffs often stopped retreating at these ridges, which the researchers described as natural speed bumps. Finally, taller cliffs tended to thin quickly as they collapsed, turning into shorter, more stable walls.

On the optimistic side, the findings suggest that the most extreme projections of sea-level rise, which depend on MICI, may need to be revised downward. That matters for governments deciding how high to build sea walls or whether to relocate whole communities, since planning for an extreme outcome that is unlikely can waste enormous sums of money. The study also shows the value of testing dramatic predictions against careful observation rather than relying on models alone.

The authors themselves, however, urge caution. Their results do not mean that Antarctica's ice sheet is safe; glaciers can still lose large amounts of ice in other ways, such as melting caused by warm ocean water, which was not the focus of this study. Moreover, four years of satellite data is a short record compared with the centuries over which ice sheets change, and conditions in a warmer future may differ from those observed so far. Needell stressed that scientists "really need to know the bed topography" and the rate at which ice is thinning in order to get ice cliff instability right.

In the end, the research replaces a simple rule with a more complicated picture. Cliff height alone does not decide a glacier's fate; the mélange, the water and the hidden landscape below all play a part. For policymakers, the message is neither panic nor complacency. Sea levels are still rising, and Antarctica will keep losing ice as the planet warms. What the new study offers is a sharper tool for estimating how fast that loss may happen, and better estimates are exactly what coastal communities need in order to prepare.

articles.title: Two Massive Stars May Be Feeding the Milky Way's Black Hole
articles.dek: Astronomers think a pair of stars may be supplying gas to the black hole at our galaxy's center, but how much should we trust an elegant explanation that nobody has watched happen?

sources.name: ScienceDaily / Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, 20 Nov 2026

paras: At the very center of our galaxy, about 26,000 light-years from Earth, lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole roughly four million times as massive as the Sun. Compared with the giant black holes that power distant quasars, it is remarkably quiet, but it is not completely asleep: it flickers and glows faintly as small amounts of gas fall toward it. Where that fuel comes from has long been a mystery. In November 2026, a team led by Stefan Gillessen of the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics in Germany proposed an intriguing answer: a pair of massive stars locked in a tight embrace.

The story begins in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of glowing gas, later named G2, racing toward the black hole on a highly stretched orbit. The cloud contained several times the mass of Earth, and it trailed a faint tail. Some researchers predicted that the black hole would flare dramatically as G2 swept past it in 2014, but no spectacular outburst occurred. That anticlimax fueled a debate over whether G2 was really a cloud of gas or a star hidden inside a dusty cocoon. Later, a search through older data revealed a similar object, G1, following almost the same path.

The new study argues that these objects are not separate clouds at all but parts of a single, continuous stream of gas. Such a stream can appear broken into clumps because the light it gives off depends very strongly on density: brightness rises with the square of the density, so the thickest parts shine while the thinner gas between them almost vanishes. The team also detected newer gas in G2's tail gathering into another clump. Together, the pieces make up what the researchers call the G1-2-3 streamer.

To reach this conclusion, the astronomers used two infrared instruments, SINFONI and ERIS, at the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile. Both rely on adaptive optics, a technology that corrects the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere. By measuring light emitted by hydrogen gas, the team tracked both the positions of the clumps and the speeds at which they move toward or away from us, and then reconstructed their orbits. The orbits of G1, G2 and G2's tail turned out to have nearly the same shape and orientation, a coincidence the researchers called extraordinarily unlikely if the clouds were unrelated.

If the gas shares a common origin, what produced it? The researchers considered several possibilities, including powerful winds from individual massive stars, stellar explosions known as novae, and material torn from passing objects by the black hole's gravity. The best match, they concluded, is IRS 16SW, a contact binary in which two massive stars orbit so closely that they almost touch. This pair belongs to a disk of young stars that circles the black hole in a clockwise direction, and the way the two stars orbit each other could explain the slight differences between the clouds' paths.

Computer simulations suggest how the system might work. Each star blows out a fierce wind of gas. Where the two winds meet, they collide and create a shock between the stars, squeezing the gas into dense clumps. Some of these clumps can break away and fall inward toward the black hole. The amount needed is surprisingly small: according to the team's calculations, if roughly one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, that could supply enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity.

Supporters see the explanation as an elegant way to tie several puzzling observations to a single cause. Instead of treating each cloud as an isolated accident, it links them to a known star system and offers a steady, ongoing source of fuel. If correct, it would also show that the behavior of an object millions of times heavier than the Sun can depend on the activity of just two nearby stars, a striking reminder that small causes can shape large systems.

Yet the researchers themselves describe their idea as plausible rather than proven, and caution is justified. The case rests largely on matching orbits and on simulations, not on directly watching gas leave IRS 16SW and fall toward the black hole. Other sources of gas may also contribute, and the long debate over G2's true nature shows how easily the galactic center can surprise astronomers. Future observations, especially of how the streamer changes over the coming decades, will be needed to test whether these two stars really are the black hole's main supplier.
